newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU drops probe into sales data row.
newsitem.headline: EU drops probe into sales data row.

text.p: The European Commission said on Tuesday it had persuaded AC Nielsen of the United States, to drop what it said were unfair practices related to the collection of sales data in Europe.

The move was a victory for rival American company Information Resources Inc, which has been trying to dent Nielsen's worldwide leadership in the market for retail tracking services ever since it launched the first scanner to register purchases at supermarket checkout counters.
It was also good news for consumer goods giants, such as Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola and Nestle, which need such services to know how their sales evolve, the Commission said in a statement.
The Commission started an investigation in May into a complaint by Information Resources that Nielsen's practices were effectively stopping it from accessing sales data in Europe.

It said on Tuesday it had dropped the probe after getting the assurance from Nielsen that it would no longer put an exclusivity clause in its contracts preventing retailers from providing data to its rivals.

Retail tracking services gather and process information on actual product sales, prices, promotions and other market data for the purpose of analysing the performance of specific products over a given period of time.
Such data were obtained manually until the introduction of scanners.
AC Nielsen is the world's leading provider of such services with a turnover of $1.3 billion in 1995, the Commission's statement said.
Information Resources, the world's second largest force on the market, gained a large share of the U.S. market after introducing its first scanner-based retail tracking service in 1986.
The dispute between the two firms is over the Nielsen practice of signing exclusivity contracts with both European retailers providing sales data and manufacturers who wanted to buy it.
"Karel Van Miert, the commissioner responsible for competition policy, has obtained an undertaking from AC Nielsen Company to modify its contractual practices," the statement said.

The Commission said Nielsen had committed itself to terminating any restrictions on retailers' freedom to supply data to other companies. Nielsen also agreed to allow multinationals to switch to a competitor in a given country without losing conditions granted in another country.

The commitments are only valid for a period of three years, however, due to the dynanimc nature of the market, the Commission said. The company will submit periodic reports to enable the EU's competition team to monitor the situation.
The Antitrust Division of the U.S. Department of Justice had also closed its own investigation into the case in view of the results achieved in Europe, the Commission said.
